title: AI Ethics in Practice: Fairness, Transparency and Accountability
subtitle: Find where bias enters AI systems, measure fairness in Python, explain and document decisions, and set up the governance and audits that keep AI accountable.
outcomes: Apply widely shared ethical principles for AI to concrete decisions about building and using AI systems
Trace where bias enters an AI system, and measure it with demographic parity, equalised odds and related measures in pandas
Explain why fairness measures can conflict, and make and document a reasoned choice between them
Explain individual decisions to the people affected, and document models with model cards
Set up accountability and governance processes, and run a fairness audit from scope to report
prerequisites: Basic Python and pandas: reading a CSV file, selecting rows and using groupby. Install Python 3 and pandas (pip install pandas). No background in ethics or law is needed.
description: Ethical AI is decided by concrete choices: what data to use, which errors to accept, who gets an explanation and who answers when things go wrong. This course turns principles into practice. You'll map the people an AI system affects and the harms it could do, trace how bias enters through historical data, under-representation, proxies and deployment, and measure fairness in pandas with selection rates, the disparate impact ratio and equalised odds. You'll see why fairness measures can't all be met at once when groups differ, and how to make and record a defensible choice. You'll explain individual decisions with reasons and counterfactuals, document a model with a model card, and apply privacy principles to AI projects. Finally, you'll set up accountability and governance, from human oversight to impact assessments, and audit a lending model's decisions by group, by threshold and at the intersection of two characteristics. The labs use a small, made-up set of loan decisions, and the course ends with a full audit report.

modules.title: Ethical principles for AI
modules.summary: Why AI ethics is a practical matter, the principles that frameworks around the world share, and how to turn them into decisions about a real system.

lessons.title: Why AI ethics is a practical matter
objectives: Describe the kinds of harm AI systems can cause
Explain why scale and feedback loops make AI harms different
key_points: AI systems can cause allocative harms, where people are unfairly given or denied opportunities and resources such as loans, jobs or housing, and representational harms, where groups are stereotyped, demeaned or made invisible.
Automated decisions operate at scale: one flawed model can repeat the same unfair decision thousands of times, faster than anyone would notice case by case.
Feedback loops can make harms grow: when a model's decisions shape the data it's retrained on, such as police patrolling where a model points, its early errors can reinforce themselves.
Documented cases show the stakes, such as the 2018 Gender Shades study, which found commercial facial-analysis systems far less accurate for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men.
Ethics in practice means concrete choices, such as what to build, which data to use, how to test and who can challenge a decision, made deliberately and recorded with their reasons.

lessons.title: Principles for trustworthy AI
objectives: Describe the principles shared by major AI ethics frameworks
Explain why principles alone don't settle hard cases
key_points: Most AI ethics frameworks share a core set of principles: fairness, transparency and explainability, accountability, privacy, safety and robustness, and human oversight.

The OECD AI Principles, adopted in 2019 and updated in 2024, were the first intergovernmental standard on AI; UNESCO's member states adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in 2021.
Principles are deliberately general, so they don't settle hard cases alone: 'be fair' doesn't say which measure of fairness to use, or who decides.
Principles can pull against each other, such as explainability against accuracy, or privacy against measuring bias, which needs data about protected characteristics.
Turning principles into practice takes processes, roles and evidence: impact assessments, testing, documentation, sign-offs and channels for complaints.

lessons.title: From principles to decisions
objectives: Identify the stakeholders affected by an AI system
Use structured questions to reach and record an ethical decision
key_points: Start with the people affected: those the system makes decisions about, those who use it, those who run it, and others, such as families or communities, who feel its effects indirectly.
For each group, ask what could go wrong, how badly, for how many people, whether they'd know, and whether they could challenge it.
Ask whether AI is the right tool at all: some decisions need human judgement, discretion or a personal relationship that a model can't provide.
Involving affected people, or those who represent them, early in design brings out harms that developers and managers are poorly placed to see.
Record the options considered, the trade-offs made and who approved them, so the decision can be reviewed and others can learn from it.

modules.title: Where bias comes from, and measuring fairness
modules.summary: Trace how bias enters a system, measure it with selection rates, the disparate impact ratio and equalised odds, and see why fairness measures can't all be satisfied at once.

lessons.title: Where bias comes from
objectives: Identify where in the machine learning life cycle bias can enter
Explain why removing a protected attribute doesn't remove bias
key_points: Historical bias is in the world the data records: a model trained on past lending or hiring decisions learns any discrimination in them, even if the data is perfectly accurate.
Representation bias arises when some groups are under-represented in the training data, so the model learns less about them and often performs worse for them.
Measurement bias arises when features or labels are poor proxies for what matters, such as arrests standing in for crime, or past health spending standing in for health needs.
Removing a protected attribute, such as race or sex, doesn't remove bias, because other features, such as postcode or income, can act as proxies for it.
Bias can also enter in evaluation, when test data doesn't reflect the people a system will serve, and in deployment, when a system is used for a purpose or population it wasn't built for.
In lending, repayment is usually seen only for people who were approved, so a model learns little about those a past policy turned away; this is called the selective labels problem.

lessons.title: Measuring fairness: demographic parity and equalised odds
objectives: Calculate selection rates, true positive rates and false positive rates by group
Apply demographic parity, the disparate impact ratio and equalised odds
key_points: A selection rate is the share of a group that gets the positive decision, such as approval; demographic parity asks for equal selection rates across groups.

The disparate impact ratio divides the lowest group's selection rate by the highest; US employment guidelines' four-fifths rule treats a ratio below 0.8 as evidence of adverse impact, a rule of thumb that prompts scrutiny, not proof.

The true positive rate (TPR) is the share of people with a good outcome, such as repaying, whom the model approves; the false positive rate (FPR) is the share of people with a bad outcome whom it approves.
Equalised odds asks for equal TPRs and equal FPRs across groups, so the model's errors fall on each group at the same rates; equal opportunity asks only for equal TPRs.
Predictive parity asks that a positive decision means the same in every group, for example that the same share of approved applicants repay in each group.
Rates from small groups are unstable, so report how many people each rate is based on, and treat differences in small samples with care.

steps.do: Load the loan decisions and look at the columns: approved is the model's decision and repaid is what actually happened.

lessons.title: Why fairness measures conflict
objectives: Explain why fairness measures can't all be met when base rates differ
Choose a fairness measure for a context and justify it
key_points: When groups have different base rates, such as different shares of applicants who repay, a model usually can't achieve demographic parity and equalised odds at the same time.

Work by Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, and by Chouldechova, showed that except in special cases, such as equal base rates or perfect prediction, a risk score can't be both equally calibrated and equal in its error rates across groups.

The debate over the COMPAS risk tool showed this in practice: ProPublica found higher false positive rates for Black defendants, while the developer argued the scores were equally calibrated for both groups.
Choosing a measure is a value judgement about which errors matter most and who bears them, so it should involve people beyond the data team, including those affected and legal advisers.

Adjusting a model to meet one measure, such as setting different thresholds for different groups, moves errors elsewhere and may itself be unlawful in some settings, so test the effects and take advice first.

lab.title: Measure fairness in loan decisions with pandas

"""Fairness measures for a lender's loan decisions, by group."""

import pandas as pd


def rates(part):
    """Selection rate, true positive rate and false positive rate for a set of applicants."""
    selection = part["approved"].mean()
    # TODO: tpr, the true positive rate: the share approved among applicants who repaid (repaid == 1)
    # TODO: fpr, the false positive rate: the share approved among applicants who didn't (repaid == 0)
    tpr = fpr = float("nan")
    return selection, tpr, fpr


def main():
    df = pd.read_csv("loans.csv")
    results = {}
    for group, part in df.groupby("group"):
        results[group] = rates(part)
        selection, tpr, fpr = results[group]
        print(f"Group {group}: {len(part)} applicants, base rate {part['repaid'].mean():.3f}, "
              f"selection rate {selection:.3f}, TPR {tpr:.3f}, FPR {fpr:.3f}")
    (sa, ta, fa), (sb, tb, fb) = results["A"], results["B"]
    # TODO: print the demographic parity difference: the gap between the two selection rates, like
    #       Demographic parity difference: 0.123
    # TODO: print the disparate impact ratio: the lower selection rate divided by the higher, like
    #       Disparate impact ratio: 0.123
    # TODO: print the equalised odds gaps: the gaps between the groups' TPRs and between their FPRs, like
    #       Equalised odds gaps: TPR 0.123, FPR 0.123


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: part.loc[part["repaid"] == 1, "approved"].mean() is the TPR: of the people who repaid, the share approved.
Real lending data rarely shows whether declined applicants would have repaid: that's the selective labels problem, and it makes TPRs and FPRs harder to measure.

modules.title: Transparency, explainability and privacy
modules.summary: Document models honestly, explain individual decisions with reasons and counterfactuals, and apply data-protection principles and privacy techniques to AI projects.

lessons.title: Transparency and documentation
objectives: Explain what transparency means for an AI system, and to whom
Describe what model cards and datasheets record
key_points: Transparency means the right people can find out what a system does: those affected need to know AI is involved and how to challenge it, while auditors and regulators need details of data, testing and limits.

A model card, proposed by Mitchell and colleagues in 2019, documents a model's intended uses, out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data, performance overall and for different groups, limitations and ethical considerations.
A datasheet for a dataset, proposed by Gebru and colleagues, records why the dataset was created, what it contains, how it was collected and labelled, and what it should and shouldn't be used for.

Telling people about AI is often a legal duty: the GDPR, for example, requires people to be told about solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, with meaningful information about the logic involved.
Documentation helps only if it's kept up to date when the model, the data or the use changes, and if it's honest about limitations.

lessons.title: Explaining model decisions
objectives: Distinguish global from local explanations
Write a plain-language explanation with reasons and a counterfactual
key_points: A global explanation describes how a model behaves overall, such as which features matter most; a local explanation says why it made one particular decision.

Simple models, such as points scorecards and small decision trees, can be explained directly; complex models need post-hoc methods, such as permutation importance, SHAP or LIME, which approximate what the model does.
Post-hoc explanations are approximations that can be unstable or misleading, so test them and don't present them as the model's exact reasoning.
A counterfactual explanation tells a person what would have had to be different for another result, such as 'with no missed payments in the past year, the application would have been approved'.

Good explanations for affected people are specific, plain and point to something they can act on or challenge; in US lending, for example, applicants refused credit are entitled to the principal reasons.

lessons.title: Privacy in AI systems
objectives: Apply data-protection principles to an AI project
Describe techniques that reduce privacy risk, and their trade-offs
key_points: Data-protection principles such as the GDPR's apply throughout an AI project: a lawful basis, a specific purpose, only the data needed, accuracy, limited retention and security.
Pseudonymised data, where names are replaced with codes, is still personal data; data counts as anonymous only when people can't be identified by any means reasonably likely to be used.
Removing names isn't enough to anonymise data: combinations such as postcode, date of birth and sex can identify many people, as re-identification studies have repeatedly shown.
Models can memorise training data and reveal it in their outputs, so personal data used in training can leak, a known risk with large generative models.
Privacy-enhancing techniques include aggregation, differential privacy (adding calibrated noise), federated learning (training where the data stays) and synthetic data, each at some cost to accuracy.
Measuring bias may need data on protected characteristics, so plan how to collect, protect and limit the use of that data rather than avoiding it altogether.

files.content:
"""Explain one decision made by the lender's points scorecard, with reasons and counterfactuals."""

THRESHOLD = 50


def score(income_k, years_in_job, missed_payments):
    """2 points per 1,000 of yearly income, 10 per year in the current job (up to 5 years), minus 15 per missed payment."""
    return 2 * income_k + 10 * min(years_in_job, 5) - 15 * missed_payments


def verdict(points):
    return "approved" if points >= THRESHOLD else "declined"


def main():
    income_k, years, missed = 22, 2, 1  # applicant L007
    points = score(income_k, years, missed)
    print(f"L007 scores {points}: {verdict(points)}")
    print(f"Years in job earn {10 * min(years, 5)} of a possible 50 points")
    print(f"Missed payments cost {15 * missed} points")
    # TODO: counterfactuals. Print the score and verdict with no missed payments, like
    #       With no missed payments: 12, declined
    # TODO: and with one more year in the job, like
    #       With one more year in the job: 12, declined
    # TODO: then find the smallest income rise, in steps of 500 a year (0.5 in thousands), that is enough
    #       for approval, and print it like:  Smallest income rise that is enough: 1500 a year


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Call score() with one input changed at a time: score(income_k, years, 0) is the no-missed-payments counterfactual.
For the income rise, start at 0 and add 0.5 (500 a year) while the score is still below THRESHOLD.

modules.title: Accountability, governance and auditing
modules.summary: Make named people answerable for AI systems, build governance processes across the life cycle, and audit a model's fairness from scope to findings.

lessons.title: Accountability and human oversight
objectives: Assign clear responsibility for an AI system
Design human oversight that works, and a route to challenge decisions
key_points: Accountability means named people answer for an AI system's outcomes: a business owner for its use, a technical owner for how it works, and a senior leader who accepts the remaining risk.

Human oversight works only if reviewers have the time, information, skills and authority to disagree with the system; otherwise it becomes rubber-stamping, made worse by automation bias, the tendency to over-trust automated advice.

People affected by significant automated decisions need a way to challenge them; the GDPR, for example, gives people safeguards including the right to obtain human intervention and to contest such decisions.
Logging inputs, outputs, model versions and human overrides makes it possible to investigate complaints and incidents afterwards.
An incident process says how problems are reported, investigated, fixed and communicated, and when to pause or switch off the system.

lessons.title: Governance processes
objectives: Describe the processes that govern AI across its life cycle
Use published frameworks to structure governance
key_points: AI governance runs across the whole life cycle: approving a new use, assessing its impact, testing before launch, monitoring in use, and reviewing or retiring the system.
An inventory of AI systems, each with an owner, a purpose and a risk rating, is the foundation: an organisation can't govern systems it doesn't know about.

Impact assessments, such as the Algorithmic Impact Assessment that Canada's government requires for its automated decision systems, ask structured questions about purpose, data, affected people and safeguards before use.
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises AI risk work into four functions, Govern, Map, Measure and Manage; ISO/IEC 42001 sets requirements for an AI management system that can be certified.
Review boards with technical, legal, business and ethics expertise can approve high-risk uses, set conditions and check that teams meet them.
Monitoring after launch checks that performance and fairness hold as data and conditions change, with thresholds that trigger a review.

lessons.title: Running a fairness audit
objectives: Plan and carry out a fairness audit of an AI system
Report findings with evidence, severity and recommendations
key_points: An audit starts with its scope and criteria: which system, which decisions, which groups, which measures and which thresholds, agreed before the results are known.
Evidence comes from documentation, data, the model's outputs on real or test cases, and interviews with the people who build it, use it and are affected by it.

Test each protected group and their intersections, such as younger applicants in one group, because a system can look acceptable for each characteristic separately and still treat an intersection badly.
Each finding states the evidence, its severity, its likely cause and a recommendation with an owner and a deadline, and the audit is followed up to check that the fixes worked.
Internal audits know the system and move faster; external audits are more independent; both need access to the data and the freedom to report unwelcome findings.

"""Audit checks: what happens to fairness measures when group B's threshold changes, and who is approved
at the intersection of group and age band."""

import pandas as pd

from fairness import rates


def main():
    df = pd.read_csv("loans.csv")
    for label, thresholds in [("Both groups at 50", {"A": 50, "B": 50}), ("Group B at 40", {"A": 50, "B": 40})]:
        # TODO: set df["approved"] to 1 where an applicant's score reaches their group's threshold, else 0.
        #       df["group"].map(thresholds) gives each applicant's threshold.
        print(label)
        for group, part in df.groupby("group"):
            selection, tpr, fpr = rates(part)
            print(f"  {group}: selection rate {selection:.3f}, TPR {tpr:.3f}, FPR {fpr:.3f}")
    df["approved"] = (df["score"] >= 50).astype(int)
    print("Selection rate by group and age band (threshold 50)")
    # TODO: group by ["group", "age_band"] and print each combination's selection rate, with how many
    #       were approved out of how many, like:  A, 30+: 0.123 (1 of 8)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: df["approved"] = (df["score"] >= df["group"].map(thresholds)).astype(int) sets the decisions for each threshold.
Equal selection rates at 40 come at a price: more group B applicants who don't repay are approved, which can harm them as well as the lender.

project.title: A fairness audit of a lending model
project.brief: The lender's board has asked for an independent-style audit of its loan scorecard before it decides whether to keep using it. Using loans.csv and the scorecard from the labs, audit the model's decisions and write a report for the board. Set the scope and criteria first; measure the model by group, by age band and at their intersections; test at least two threshold options and explain their trade-offs; review its transparency (with a model card and a sample explanation for a declined applicant); and cover privacy, accountability and governance: how protected-attribute data is handled, who oversees decisions, how applicants can challenge them and what is monitored. End with a recommendation to keep, change or stop the model, stating the trade-offs openly. The data is made up, so be clear about what a real audit would need that this data can't show.
deliverables: Scope and criteria: the decisions, groups, measures and thresholds, and why you chose them
Your Python code and its output: measures by group, by age band and at intersections, and at least two threshold options
A results table and three to six findings, each with evidence, severity, likely cause, recommendation and owner
A model card and a sample explanation for a declined applicant
A privacy, accountability and governance section
An overall recommendation with its trade-offs, and the limits of this audit
